subject: Banking
title: How Cash Moves Through an Economy
description: One-minute skill: How Cash Moves Through an Economy.

hook.text: A single $20 bill changes hands about 55 times per year. Each exchange creates economic activity worth far more.

buildup.text: This is the velocity of money. The faster cash circulates, the more economic output the same dollars generate.

discovery.text: Central banks track velocity closely. When people hoard cash, velocity drops and the economy slows down.

twist.text: During COVID, velocity collapsed to historic lows. People saved instead of spending. Recovery took massive stimulus.

climax.text: Cash is not just currency. It is a measurement of economic confidence and activity in real time.

punchline.text: One bill, 55 transactions per year. Cash velocity drives economies.

quiz.question: What does 'velocity of money' measure?
options: How often each unit of currency changes hands in a period

details.summary: Physical cash circulates from the central bank to commercial banks to businesses to consumers and back, with worn notes destroyed and replaced, creating a continuous loop that costs billions to maintain annually.
details.whyItMatters: Cash infrastructure is enormously expensive. Understanding the full lifecycle of physical money reveals why governments and banks are eager to shift toward cheaper digital payment alternatives.
takeaways: Central banks print new notes and destroy worn ones continuously
Armored trucks, ATMs, and vault storage cost billions annually
Cash in circulation has actually increased despite digital payment growth

faq.question: How long does a typical banknote last?
faq.answer: It depends on denomination. A US one-dollar bill lasts about 6 years. Higher denominations last 10 to 15 years because they are handled less frequently. Polymer notes used in many countries last 2 to 3 times longer than paper.

faq.question: Why is cash in circulation growing if everyone uses cards?
faq.answer: Much of the growth is in large-denomination bills used for savings, especially in unstable economies, and for shadow economy transactions. Cash as a store of value is growing even as cash for daily payments declines.
